bottleneck: Cas9 comes from common bacteria (Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus), so many humans carry pre-existing antibodies and T-cells against it. Delivering Cas9 protein or expressing it in vivo can therefore trigger immune clearance of the editor before it finishes working, or immune attack on edited cells afterward. Repeated dosing — likely needed for many therapies — amplifies the problem.
current_state: Immune-evasive Cas variants, transient immunosuppression, and mRNA-based transient expression are being tested, but no standard solution exists for in vivo Cas9 delivery.

sources.title: CRISPR Unleashed: Engineering Our Next-Gen Antivirals

title: Pre-existing immunity to Cas9 limits in vivo editing
why_it_blocks: An editor the immune system recognizes is an editor that gets destroyed mid-job. Until Cas immunity is managed, in vivo editing must either hide from immunity or restrict itself to immune-privileged sites and ex vivo workflows.
